body:
So I don't think we support junctions, though we do (or try to) support symlinks.

If you run Syncthing as administrator on Windows, the symlink should get synced properly.

The reason it gets ignored is most likely because of not having permissions to create one.
The fact that you cannot create one is probably the reason you get these issues.
Are there any useful information in the console logs?

Issue 1017 is more like a kill switch if you don't want to sync symlinks at all, but it's off by default.

Hi @AudriusButkevicius - the issue is more to do with Windows Node being 'Up to Date' regardless of what symbolic links I have created (as admin or not  and as junction or via mklink). But when a symbolic link is created on Linux - then the Node status on that computer changes from 'Up to Date'  to 'Syncing (100%)'.  This (as per my scenarios described) happen regardless of the symbolic links existing or not on the other Windows node.

I will try the same again but with Syncthing ruining as administrator on Windows - as see if it makes any difference. At the moment it run under my user (started in a cli window).

Well at the point one of the nodes cannot create symlinks, all bets are off, and if the windows node has the link, it will show up as 100% as there is nothing for it todo, but if the linux node created the link, the windows node might look out of sync as it's unable to create the link.

The fact that the symlink is created by hand might not work, as we have a few pieces of metadata in syncthing about the symlinks, and if those for some reason don't match, it will look out of sync.

If you want to create symlinks by hand, enable config.xml on both sides to disable symlink support, and try again (might need to zap the index, not sure).

@AudriusButkevicius I have re-check the manual creation of symbolic links as I described earlier, but with Syncthing running under a administrator cli instead on Windows. 

The results are slightly different:
1. Any symbolic links manual created on the Linux computer (when they dont exists on Windows) - now get successfully replicated to the Windows computer.
2. However, any symbolic links manual created on the Windows computer (when they dont exists on Linux) - do not get  replicated to the  Linux computer (see messages seen on the Linux computer below).
3. In both the above though - the Node status remains 'Up to Date' - so having Syncthing running as  administrator on Windows does change the way the Linux computer reports the Windows Nodes sync status.

The messages below are seen on the Linux box - and it does instead show the Windows Node at 'Up to Date' - which is different to before. The Windows box shows no 'Notice' messages, and it is 'Up to Date' also - basically same behavior for Windows from a status reporting perspective.

'Notice' appearing on the Linux Node:

```
10:28:57: puller: final: creating symlink: symlink /datastore/SyncData/MoonStore/Development-Code/WebSites/hugo-wiremoons.com/public: no such file or directory

10:28:57: puller: final: creating symlink: symlink /datastore/SyncData/MoonStore/Development-Code/WebSites/hugo-wiremoons.com/public: no such file or directory

10:28:57: Folder "MoonStore" isn't making progress - check logs for possible root cause. Pausing puller for 1m0s.
```

So am I right to assume that the symlinks from Windows get created on Unix, but you get a bunch of warnings?

Yeah, definitely something weird is happening.
I tested `Win <-> Win` before we introduced some changes.
I'll check `Win <-> Unix` later today or tomorrow, as it seems we've missed something.

_So am I right to assume that the symlinks from Windows get created on Unix, but you get a bunch of warnings?_

**Answer:** No - not quite. Have summarised below based on what I have tested,  and results from following your suggestions. Hope it makes more sense then :)

## First test performed:

Syncthing running as a **User** on Windows and **no Symbolic links exists on either system**.

Create symbolic link on Windows.
- Windows fine, symbolic link works on Windows ok. **No symlink replication to Unix though.**
- Windows computer repo 'Up to Date' its view of the Unix computer is 'Up to Date'
- Unix computer repo 'Up to Date' its view of the Windows computer is 'Up to Date'
- No 'Notice' messages on either computer

Now manually add same symbolic link on Unix.
- Windows fine, symbolic link works on Windows ok as before - no change
- Windows computer repo 'Up to Date' its view of the Unix computer is 'Up to Date'
- Unix computer repo 'Up to Date' **BUT** its view of the Windows computer is 'Syncing (100%)'

The above stays like that unless the Unix computer removes its symbolic link. The removal does not replicate to the Windows computer though - due to lack of Admin privileges for Syncthing on Windows - as you pointed out maybe? But the Node and Repo status do then return to 'Up to Date'.

## Second test performed:

Syncthing running as a **Administrator** on Windows and **no Symbolic links exists on either system**.

Create symbolic link on Windows.
- Windows fine, symbolic link works on Windows ok. **No symlink replication to Unix though.**
- Windows computer repo 'Up to Date' its view of the Unix computer is 'Syncing (100%)'
- Unix computer repo 'Up to Date - **1 item Out of Sync**' its view of the Windows computer is 'Up to Date'
- 'Notice' messages appear only on Unix computer as posted earlier.

Now manually add same symbolic link on Unix.
- Windows fine, symbolic link works on Windows ok as before - no change
- Windows computer repo 'Up to Date'  and its view of the Unix computer is 'Up to Date'
- Unix computer repo 'Up to Date' and its view of the Windows computer is 'Up to Date'

If the Unix computer removes its symbolic link - the removal is replicated to the Windows computer now too. Also if the Unix computer re-creates the symbolic link - it is also replicated to the Windows computer too. So this behavior is great. It just doen't work replicating the initial symbolic link creation from Windows to Unix?

My guess is there is a bug(s)
1. `windows -> unix` replication?
2. strange Node and repo status reporting as a result of issue 1?
3. Windows only works well with replicating Unix symbolic links if it is run under Admin?

Hope that helps :)

The first scenario and bug 3 is not a bug.
You can only create symlinks when running as admin, so if you are not running as admin, we don't even attempt to create them, and show you the warning about not running as Administrator, so the `Syncthing (100%)` is expected, and working as intended.

1 and 2 do seem like there is some issue.

OK - just to be clear:
- _first scenario_ - this is dependent on Unix not Windows (ie `Windows -> Unix`). The symbolic link is created fine on Windows (the user makes it) - but it is not replicated on the Unix host though. The Unix host should see Windows made a new symbolic link - and make one itself on the Unix system? No Windows privileges apply to the Unix host - it just replicates the symbolic link?  It works this way now (ie the other way around) when Syncthing is run under Administrator the Unix symbolic links are replicated straight onto Windows.
- 'bug 3' _Windows only works well with replicating Unix symbolic links if it is run under Admin?_ - agreed for replicating a new link on Windows - where one was made on Unix. Not sure what code Syncthing uses to create symbolic links - see some comments and observation below. But I agree.

Running Windows Syncthing as Administrator - specifically for the symbolic link creation privileges needed in a `cmd.exe` cli window I noticed the following while testing:
1. The creation of symbolic links for Windows using `mklink` requires Admin privileges. Advantage of `mklink` is this works for symbolic link creation for files and directories 
2. The creation of symbolic links for **directories only** can be done with [junction.exe](http://technet.microsoft.com/en-gb/sysinternals/bb896768.aspx) - and this does not need Admin privileges!  Advantage is that can create symbolic link directories as a user. Disadvantage is can not create symbolic links for files.

Not sure how the two differ - or why `junction.exe` can create directory symbolic links without Admin - but `mklink` can not...

As both are from Microsoft guess it maybe some internal code voodoo :)  I also know `mklink` is built into `cmd.exe` as it does not work in PowerShell - but junction.exe works in both, as it is a separate program.

Also not sure how or which approach Syncthing uses?  I did post last week about Go 1.4 including symbolic link support in Windows now (thanks for you response by the way!) - is it doing anything different to `mklink` to do this?

Just curious - I know you said this is already sorted in the other message. I could go read the code I guess :)

Simon

Junction is not a symbolic link, and Go's standard API doesn't even have a call for creating junctions.

The implementation that came into Go 1.4 is pretty blunt and only works when the target of the symlink is known.
If you create a symlink to a non-existing target it will default to creating a file symlink, which might not be valid if the target then later appears to be a directory. The only way to fix this is to remove the symlink and recreate it.
This is obviously not true for Unix, as symlinks don't have a type and don't care about the target.
Hence why we need to roll out our own custom implementation to jump the hoops introduced by Windows.

I am not going to resort to an implementation which calls some random utility which was shipped with some versions of the OS just to be able to create one of the two types of `symlinks` without the need of administrator privileges.

It's a feature which you can choose to use or not to use, it's up to you, but you'll need to do your bit (running as admin) if you choose to use it.

I agree @AudriusButkevicius - I wasnt suggesting you did '_call some random utility_' - dont worry :)
I was just interested - so thanks for the explanation!
